feed.title: Combined summary - Handling PQ signatures on the stack

entry.title: Combined summary - Handling PQ signatures on the stack
entry.summary: Support for post-quantum (PQ) signatures in Bitcoin, such as SHRINCS, necessitates reconsideration of the current 520-byte stack element size limit. Present cryptographic schemes that offer post-quantum security typically produce signatures far exceeding this constraint, with the exception of isogeny-based approaches. To address this, a proposal exists to raise the tapscript stack element size limit to 6 kilobytes, as detailed in a [SHRINCS BIP draft](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76). This adjustment aims to accommodate larger PQ signatures within the scripting system and is being discussed in collaboration with P2MR developers. The rationale for increasing the limit is under active review, and further discourse continues on the [project’s issue tracker](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/issues/3). Permitting large stack elements introduces significant denial-of-service (DoS) risks for Bitcoin nodes. Scripting operations can duplicate or hash these sizable elements, leading to substantial increases in CPU resource consumption compared to the status quo. Hash functions like `OP_RIPEMD160` are particularly problematic due to their lack of hardware acceleration, while operations such as `OP_VERIFY`, `OP_IFDUP`, and `OP_EQUAL` must scan stack elements byte by byte, which can be slow when dealing with large data, especially if operated on repeatedly. Several strategies are under consideration for safely handling large stack elements: One approach is chunking, which retains the 520-byte consensus limit but expects new opcodes requiring more data to concatenate multiple stack elements. While this method avoids changes to implementation performance and consensus rules, it imposes complex requirements at the user and wallet level. Parsing and constructing transactions would require intricate logic to manage chunked data, and scripting could become convoluted. Moreover, there is a minor overhead from length encoding for each chunk, although this is negligible relative to PQ signature sizes. Another possibility is opcode blacklisting, where certain script operations are restricted from acting on elements larger than 520 bytes. Signature-checking opcodes would be explicitly permitted for large elements, but duplication and similar operations might be disallowed or subject to strict limits. This reduces DoS vectors by preventing repeated manipulation of large elements, but it also curtails scripting flexibility, possibly hindering some covenant designs and unexplored use cases involving large non-signature data. Careful analysis is required to ensure that remaining opcodes do not create new vulnerabilities. A thorough solution involves optimizing implementations to minimize the runtime cost of processing large stack elements. By profiling all relevant opcodes and targeting the most computationally expensive ones, various optimizations could be applied, such as hash caching, pointer representations for stack elements, and caching truthiness checks. These improvements can enhance validation performance and are decoupled from consensus, allowing immediate progress. However, the burden on node software increases, and maintaining robust DoS resistance demands ongoing vigilance. The introduction of GSR’s variable operations budget, as proposed in [BIP-440](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/9f3d3bc6a60db16efbdc71ac8f7ea30217fc0c39/bip-0440.mediawiki), represents another avenue. This framework would enforce compute and memory usage limits directly through consensus: scripts exceeding their allocated resources would simply fail. When paired with [BIP-441](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/9f3d3bc6a60db16efbdc71ac8f7ea30217fc0c39/bip-0441.mediawiki), this method preserves and potentially expands scripting capabilities, albeit at the cost of increased protocol complexity and extensive testing. Alternatively, establishing a dedicated “signature stack” isolates large signature data from general script manipulation. Only specific opcodes, such as CHECKSIG, could access this stack, which eliminates interpreter-level DoS risks for other operations. While conceptually clean, this approach discards the ability to manipulate signatures within scripts, diverging from traditional semantics and limiting flexibility. Hybrid solutions are also conceivable, combining implementation optimizations with targeted consensus changes. For instance, using pointers to represent stack elements can standardize operation costs, while blacklisting only those opcodes most susceptible to abuse, like hashing or scanning. Among these options, chunking is regarded as unnecessarily complex given that upgradable tapscript limits allow for more principled solutions. Opcode blacklisting is seen as counterproductive if the aim is to enable novel uses of large signature data within scripts. Pure optimization, while enticing for its technical challenges, risks missing edge cases that could undermine DoS protection. The varops budget model offers a comprehensive and future-proof answer for enabling flexible scripts with large data, whereas an isolated signature stack provides a straightforward interim solution for supporting PQ signatures without expanding the scripting surface exposed to DoS threats.
